title: A Car for Every Purse: GM, the Beetle and the World's Carmakers
summary: General Motors beat Ford by letting people choose: cheap cars, fancy cars, new styles every year, and paying a little each month. Around the world, clever designers made tiny, cheerful cars like the Mini, the 2CV and the Volkswagen Beetle. Then a Japanese company called Toyota found a smarter way to build cars, and its Corolla became the best-selling car name of all time.

sections.heading: Billy Durant's Car Collection
paragraphs: While Henry Ford was perfecting one car, another man in Michigan was collecting whole car companies the way some people collect trading cards. His name was William C. Durant, and everybody called him Billy.

Durant did not start with cars at all. In 1886, in the town of Flint, Michigan, he and a partner named Josiah Dallas Dort founded a company that built horse-drawn road carts. By the early 1900s their Durant-Dort Carriage Company had become one of the biggest makers of horse-drawn vehicles in the United States. Durant was a brilliant salesman who understood that people bought vehicles through dealers, on trust, and on dreams.

In 1904 he took control of a struggling young carmaker called Buick and used his carriage company's money, factories and dealer network to turn it around. Within a few years Buick was one of the best-selling cars in America. Durant had a bigger idea. Instead of betting everything on one car, why not own many car companies, so that if one model failed, the others would carry on?

On 16 September 1908, just a couple of weeks before Ford introduced the Model T, Durant founded General Motors. Within about a year GM had bought Oldsmobile, Cadillac and the Oakland Motor Car Company (whose cars were later sold as Pontiac), along with many smaller firms making parts. Durant was a dreamer, though, not a careful accountant. He spent so fast that GM ran short of cash, and in 1910 the bankers who lent it money pushed him out.

Durant bounced back. In 1911 he teamed up with Louis Chevrolet, a Swiss-born racing driver, to start a new car company bearing Chevrolet's name. Chevrolet the man soon left after disagreements, but Chevrolet the car became a hit. Durant used its success to buy up GM shares and, amazingly, regained control of General Motors in 1916, and in 1918 Chevrolet officially joined the GM family. Then, in 1920, during a sudden business slump, he lost control again, this time for good, to the du Pont family and other big investors.

Durant's later life is a reminder that business can be a roller coaster. He started more companies, lost most of his fortune in the stock market crash and the Great Depression, and in his old age ran a bowling alley with a small restaurant in Flint. But the giant he had assembled was about to be reorganised by a very different kind of leader.

sections.heading: Alfred Sloan's Ladder of Cars
paragraphs: Alfred P. Sloan was an engineer from New York who had run a company making roller bearings, the small hardened steel balls and rollers that let wheels and shafts spin smoothly. When his firm became part of the GM group in the 1910s, he joined General Motors, and in 1923 he became its president. Where Durant was a gambler, Sloan was an organiser. He loved charts, numbers and clear rules.

Sloan looked at GM's messy family of brands, several of which were competing against one another for the same buyers, and sorted them into a neat ladder of prices. At the bottom was Chevrolet, a low-priced car meant to fight the Model T. Above it came Pontiac, then Oldsmobile, then Buick, and at the very top the luxurious Cadillac. GM described the idea as offering a car for every purse and purpose, meaning a car for every budget and every need.

The ladder worked like a staircase through life. A young couple might buy a Chevrolet. As they earned more, they could step up to a Pontiac or Oldsmobile, then to a Buick, and perhaps one day a Cadillac, without ever leaving GM. Compare that with Ford's approach: for years, Ford essentially offered one car, in one basic design, eventually in one color.

Sloan's second big idea was the yearly model change. Each year, GM cars received new styling, new trim and small improvements, so that last year's car looked a little old-fashioned. Supporters called this progress; critics later called it planned obsolescence, meaning deliberately making products seem out of date so people buy new ones sooner. Either way, it got customers excited every autumn when the new models arrived.

The third idea was buying on credit. In 1919 GM set up the General Motors Acceptance Corporation, known as GMAC, which lent money to customers so they could drive a car home after paying only part of the price, then pay the rest in monthly instalments. Henry Ford disliked debt and was slow to follow. For millions of families, being able to pay bit by bit made a new car possible years sooner.

The fourth idea was style. In 1927 a young Californian designer named Harley Earl, who had built flashy custom car bodies for Hollywood stars, designed the elegant LaSalle for GM's Cadillac division. It was such a success that Sloan created a special department, the Art and Colour Section, and made Earl its first leader. It was one of the first in-house design departments at any big carmaker. Earl pioneered shaping new car designs in modelling clay, so designers could see and change the curves in three dimensions. His team built the Buick Y-Job around 1938 to 1939, often called the first concept car, a show car built to test the public's reaction. Later, GM's 1948 Cadillac carried small tailfins inspired by a fighter plane, the Lockheed P-38 Lightning, starting a fashion that grew wilder through the 1950s.

Earl also had a secret project for a sporty two-seater. Chevrolet's managers liked it, and in 1953 the public met the Chevrolet Corvette, a low, open sports car with a body moulded from fibreglass, a lightweight material made of glass fibres set in plastic resin. It showed that even the company famous for sensible family cars could sell excitement, and the Corvette is still being made today, more than seventy years later.

In 1927, the year Ford shut down to switch from the Model T to the Model A, Chevrolet sold more cars in the United States than Ford did, by most counts. Ford fought back, and the two brands traded first place for decades, but General Motors as a whole grew into the largest industrial company the world had ever seen. Sloan's ladder, yearly models, credit and styling became the standard way to sell cars almost everywhere.

sections.heading: Small Wonders: Europe's Tiny Cars
paragraphs: In Europe, life was different. Roads were often narrow and twisty, cities were old and crowded, fuel was expensive, and many governments taxed cars by engine size. Most families had far less money than American families. So European designers became experts at something difficult: making a car as small, light and cheap as possible while still fitting a family inside.

In Britain, Herbert Austin, with a young draughtsman named Stanley Edge helping on the detailed drawings, created the Austin 7, announced in July 1922. Its four-cylinder engine was tiny, only 696 cc at first and 747 cc from 1923, smaller than many of today's motorcycle engines, and made only about 10 horsepower. Yet it was a proper little car with four wheels, real brakes and room for a small family. People called it the Baby Austin. About 290,000 were built in Britain until 1939, and the design was built under licence or copied abroad: in Germany as the Dixi, the first car made by BMW, in France by Rosengart and in the United States as the American Austin. It also helped end the craze for flimsy, half-motorcycle cyclecars.

In France, Pierre-Jules Boulanger, a leader of the Citroën company, asked his engineers in the 1930s for a car that would bring motoring to French farmers. According to the famous brief, it should be like an umbrella on four wheels, carry four people and about 50 kg of farm goods, and drive across a freshly ploughed field without breaking a basket of eggs. André Lefèbvre led the engineering, and others including Flaminio Bertoni and Walter Becchia shaped its body and engine. When Germany invaded France during World War II, Citroën staff hid the prototypes from the occupying forces; some were buried or destroyed so they could not be used.

The car finally appeared at the Paris Motor Show on 7 October 1948. It was the Citroën 2CV, short for deux chevaux, two horses, which referred to its tiny rating in the French tax system. Its first engine was a 375 cc air-cooled twin of about 9 horsepower. Its soft, bouncy suspension let it lean dramatically in corners, and the roof was a roll-back canvas sheet. Critics laughed, but buyers queued for years. Production lasted until 1990, and more than 3.8 million 2CVs were built.

In Italy, Fiat engineer Dante Giacosa designed the Nuova 500, launched in July 1957. It was under 3 metres long, about 2.97 m, with a 479 cc two-cylinder air-cooled engine at the back. Italians nicknamed it the Cinquecento, meaning five hundred. It squeezed families into narrow medieval streets and parked in gaps where bigger cars could not fit. Nearly 3.9 million were made before production ended in 1975.

Britain's most famous small car came out of a fuel crisis. In 1956 the Suez Crisis disrupted oil supplies, and Britain brought in petrol rationing. Tiny German bubble cars suddenly sold well. The British Motor Corporation asked its designer Alec Issigonis to create a proper small car that used little fuel. His answer, announced on 26 August 1959, was the Mini.

Issigonis's trick was to turn the engine sideways. Instead of pointing front to back, the four-cylinder engine sat across the car, a layout called transverse, with the gearbox tucked underneath it in the oil sump, driving the front wheels. With no long engine in front and no driveshaft running to the back, about 80 percent of the floor space could be used for people and luggage, even though the car was only about 3.05 metres long. Tiny 10-inch wheels sat right at the corners. The Mini went around corners like a go-kart, and sporty Mini Coopers won the famous Monte Carlo Rally in 1964, 1965 and 1967. About 5.4 million original Minis were built before production ended in 2000. Today, most small family cars in the world use the same idea of a sideways engine driving the front wheels.

sections.heading: The Beetle: A People's Car with a Dark Beginning
paragraphs: The most famous small car of all has a complicated story, and it is worth telling honestly. In the 1930s, Germany was ruled by the Nazi government led by Adolf Hitler. The government wanted a cheap Volkswagen, which simply means people's car in German, to win popularity with ordinary Germans, and it hired the engineer Ferdinand Porsche, whom you met in Part 7, to develop it. Hitler did not design the car. Porsche and his engineering team did, and historians note that other designers in Europe had been sketching similar small, rounded, rear-engined cars before them, so exactly who deserves credit for which idea is still debated.

The design was unusual. The engine sat at the back, not the front. It was a flat-four, meaning four cylinders lying flat, two on each side, and it was cooled by air blown over metal fins instead of by water and a radiator, so there was no water to freeze in winter or boil over in summer. The body had a rounded shape that helped it slip through the air, and the car was built to cruise steadily on Germany's new motorways.

Ordinary Germans were encouraged to pay into a savings scheme, a few marks every week, toward their own car. A huge new factory was built from 1938 near the village of Fallersleben, beside a new town later named Wolfsburg. But World War II began in 1939, and the factory switched to building military vehicles, such as the Kübelwagen, an army version of the car, instead. More than 330,000 people who had paid into the savings scheme never received a car. During the war, as in many German factories, much of the work was done by forced labourers and prisoners brought from occupied countries, a painful chapter that Volkswagen has since acknowledged and studied.

By the end of the war in 1945 the factory was heavily damaged by bombing, and it lay in the zone of Germany controlled by the British army. It might easily have been taken apart. Instead, a young British officer named Major Ivan Hirst, an engineer in the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers, arrived in the summer of 1945 and saw that much of the machinery had survived. The occupying forces badly needed vehicles, so Hirst persuaded the British military to order 20,000 cars from the factory. Working with German staff in a half-ruined building, often short of parts and materials, the factory was producing about 1,000 cars a month by 1946.

British carmakers who inspected the car at the time were not impressed and thought it had no future. They were spectacularly wrong. In 1948 Heinrich Nordhoff, a German manager, took charge, and in 1949 control passed to the new West German government. Volkswagen began exporting all over the world. In the United States, an advertising campaign from 1959 with the slogan Think Small turned the car's tiny size into a joke that made people like it more. People everywhere called it the Beetle, the Bug, the Käfer in German, or the Fusca in Brazil.

The Beetle kept its basic shape for decades while being improved underneath. On 17 February 1972, it passed the Ford Model T's record of about 15 million cars to become the most-produced car model in the world up to that time. Production moved between factories in Germany, Brazil, Mexico and elsewhere. The very last original Beetle rolled off the line in Puebla, Mexico, on 30 July 2003. In total, about 21.5 million were made, a car born in one of the darkest periods of the twentieth century that ended up becoming a friendly symbol of peace and fun.

sections.heading: Car Factories Go to War
paragraphs: During World War II, car factories in many countries were turned to military work, because they were the best places on Earth for making complicated machines in huge numbers. In the United States, which joined the war at the end of 1941, the government ordered carmakers to stop building cars for ordinary customers in early 1942. For more than three years, almost no new family cars were built in America.

Instead, the assembly lines built trucks, tanks, aircraft engines, guns and shells. General Motors, Ford and Chrysler became some of the biggest military suppliers in the country. Chrysler ran an enormous tank factory near Detroit. Other companies built engines for fighter planes. The small, tough Jeep, built by Willys-Overland and by Ford, became one of the war's best-known vehicles.

The most dramatic example was Ford's Willow Run plant near Ypsilanti, Michigan. It was designed by Albert Kahn, the same architect who had designed Highland Park, and Charles Sorensen led the effort to plan it. Willow Run was gigantic, with roughly 3.5 million square feet of floor space, more than 300,000 square metres, and at its peak about 42,000 people worked there. Its job was to build the B-24 Liberator, a big four-engine bomber, far more complicated than any car.

At first, Willow Run struggled. Airplanes were far more complicated than cars, and the designs kept changing. Critics joked about it. But by 1944 the plant was finishing a bomber roughly every hour, about one every 63 minutes at its best, and in a single month it produced more than 400. By the end of the war Ford had built about 7,000 complete B-24s there and supplied kits for nearly 1,900 more. Willow Run became a symbol of how mass-production ideas from the Model T era could be applied to almost anything.

When the war ended in 1945, the factories switched back to cars, and Americans who had waited years for a new car rushed to buy one. In Europe and Japan, by contrast, many factories had been damaged or destroyed. Rebuilding them would take years, and in Japan it would lead to a very different way of building cars.

sections.heading: Toyota and the Smarter Factory
paragraphs: Toyota's story begins not with cars but with weaving looms, the machines that turn thread into cloth. Sakichi Toyoda was a Japanese inventor who designed clever automatic looms, including one that stopped by itself when a thread broke, so that faulty cloth was not produced and one worker could watch many machines. His son, Kiichiro Toyoda, was an engineer who dreamed of building cars.

In 1933 Kiichiro set up an automobile department inside the family's loom company. His team studied American and European cars, taking them apart to learn how they worked, and completed their first passenger car prototype, the Model A1, in May 1935. In 1937 the car business became a separate company, the Toyota Motor Co. The family name is Toyoda, but the company chose the spelling Toyota, reportedly partly because it was considered luckier and sounded clearer.

Japan after World War II was poor, and Toyota nearly went bankrupt around 1950. Kiichiro Toyoda resigned as president that year during a labour dispute, and he died in 1952. Toyota could not copy Ford's approach of building one model in vast numbers with mountains of spare parts piled up in warehouses. It did not have the money, the space or the customers. It needed to build many different vehicles, in smaller numbers, without wasting anything.

The engineer who worked out how was Taiichi Ohno, together with Eiji Toyoda, a cousin of Kiichiro. Over about three decades, from the late 1940s to the 1970s, they developed what became known as the Toyota Production System. One of its two main ideas was just-in-time: making only what is needed, only when it is needed, and only in the amount needed. Ohno was inspired partly by American supermarkets, where shelves are refilled only as customers take things away. In a Toyota factory, each station takes the parts it needs from the station before it, and that station then makes just enough to replace them. Simple cards called kanban travel with the parts to signal what to make next.

The other main idea came straight from Sakichi's looms. It is called jidoka, often translated as automation with a human touch. If something goes wrong, the line stops so the problem can be found and fixed at once, instead of letting faulty cars pile up at the end of the line to be repaired later. Workers could signal a problem, and a lighted board called an andon showed supervisors exactly where help was needed. In Ford's old system, stopping the line was almost unthinkable. In Toyota's, it was part of the job.

Toyota also encouraged workers to suggest small improvements every day, a habit called kaizen, which means continuous improvement. Over time, these ideas made Toyota's cars famous for reliability. Researchers in the West later studied the system in detail and gave it the name lean manufacturing, and today hospitals, offices and software companies borrow its ideas.

In November 1966 Toyota launched a small family car called the Corolla, with a 1.1-litre engine. It was not flashy. It was simply comfortable, affordable and very hard to break. When the oil crisis of 1973, which you will read about in Part 17, made fuel expensive, small, efficient and reliable Japanese cars like the Corolla won buyers all over the world. In 1997 the Corolla passed the Beetle's total, and in 2021 Toyota announced that more than 50 million Corollas had been sold across twelve generations. That makes it the best-selling car name in history.

sections.heading: A World Full of Carmakers
paragraphs: Look back over this part and you can see a pattern. Ford showed that a car could be cheap if you built one design in enormous numbers. General Motors showed that people also wanted choice, style and easy payments. European designers showed that clever engineering could fit a family into a very small, thrifty car. Volkswagen showed that a simple design, improved patiently, could last for generations. And Toyota showed that a factory could be fast, flexible and careful about quality all at once.

By the 1980s, cars were being built on every inhabited continent. Germany, France, Italy, Britain, Sweden, Japan and the United States had big car industries, and countries such as South Korea, Brazil and Mexico were building more and more. Factories that once made a few hundred cars a year now made hundreds of thousands. The number of cars on the world's roads climbed into the hundreds of millions.

The competitors also learned from each other. Ford eventually adopted yearly models, a range of brands and credit for buyers. General Motors and other Western companies later studied Toyota's methods closely, and some even ran joint factories with Toyota to learn them first-hand. Japanese and European firms, in turn, borrowed American marketing and styling ideas. No single company or country had all the answers; the modern car industry grew out of this constant copying, competing and improving, just as the car itself had been built from the ideas of many inventors.

Every one of those cars needed somewhere to go. Each one wanted a smooth surface, signposts, rules about who goes first, places to fill up with fuel and places to park. So with millions of new cars pouring out of factories every year, a big question loomed: where on earth were they all going to drive?

deepDive: Business historians often present the Ford–GM rivalry of the 1920s as a contest between two philosophies. Ford's strategy was cost leadership through a single standardised product: highly specialised machinery drove the cost of a Model T down, but made change expensive. Sloan's GM used a multidivisional structure, in which brands such as Chevrolet and Cadillac ran their own operations while a central office set financial targets and coordinated the price ladder. This model, analysed by the historian Alfred Chandler, became a template for large corporations in many industries. Yearly model changes and consumer credit are still debated: they made cars accessible and fuelled innovation in styling and engineering, but they also encouraged debt and quick replacement of products that still worked. The Volkswagen story raises different questions about memory and responsibility. The car was promoted by a dictatorship, the savings scheme failed its subscribers, and the wartime factory relied on forced labour; yet the postwar company, revived under British supervision, became a central part of West Germany's economic recovery. Historians commissioned by Volkswagen in the 1990s documented the wartime forced labour in detail. Toyota's contribution is now one of the most studied topics in management. Researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology compared car plants around the world in the 1980s and concluded that lean Japanese plants could build a car with far fewer labour-hours and fewer defects than many Western mass-production plants, which helped spread just-in-time and quality methods. Critics point out that just-in-time systems are vulnerable when supply chains break, as the global shortage of computer chips showed in 2021, when carmakers around the world had to halt production because a few small parts were missing. Numbers also need care: production totals for the Beetle, the Mini and other long-lived models vary slightly between sources, depending on whether foreign assembly and close variants are counted.
funFact: Citroën's design brief for the 2CV asked that it be able to drive across a ploughed field carrying a basket of eggs without breaking any.
